issues.legal_issue: A landlord may remain in legal possession of residential premises while living elsewhere if the premises are retained under the landlord’s control.
material_facts: The landlady lived in another town and did not actually reside in the premises at the time.
The premises were locked and contained her household effects.
issues.conclusion: The landlady’s absence from the premises did not mean that she was not in possession of them; her possession remained sufficient for the landlord-nomination provision to apply.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, occupation for residential purposes is not limited to an owner’s physical presence. A landlord may retain possession while away by keeping household effects in locked premises or leaving the premises in another’s charge. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.rent_control_allotment_proceeding: The matter concerned the allotment of premises that had become vacant under a rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_resided_elsewhere: The landlord lived elsewhere rather than physically residing in the premises.
predicates.landlord_retained_control_of_premises: The landlord kept the premises under their control, including by leaving household effects there or keeping them locked.

issues.definition: When an allotment proceeding concerns premises retained under a landlord’s control despite the landlord living elsewhere, the landlord remains in legal possession.

issues.legal_issue: A rent-control authority cannot allot a newly vacant part of a building to someone other than the landlord’s nominee without giving the landlord an opportunity to nominate a tenant when the statutory conditions for nomination are met.
material_facts: A tenant gave notice that he intended to vacate premises forming part of a building associated with the landlady’s residential occupation.
The authority allotted the premises to the appellant without informing the landlady or asking her to nominate a tenant.
The landlady was not living in the premises, but they were locked and contained her household effects.
The landlady’s request to release the premises was not granted, and the authorities nevertheless re-allotted them to the appellant without giving her an opportunity to nominate a tenant.
issues.conclusion: The allotment to the appellant was without jurisdiction because the authorities did not comply with the landlord’s nomination entitlement; the High Court was justified in quashing the orders and remanding the matter for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires allotment of the remaining part of a building to a person nominated by the landlord where the statutory residential-occupation or release conditions apply. The provision protects the landlord from having an unwanted tenant or neighbour imposed on them. A refusal of release under Section 16(1)(b) does not excuse the authorities from complying with Section 17(2). No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.rent_control_vacancy_allotment_proceedin: The matter concerned an authority’s allotment of premises that had become vacant in a building subject to rent control.
predicates.landlord_entitled_to_nominate: The landlord occupied another part of the building for residential purposes, or the relevant part had been released to the landlord for residential purposes, so the landlord was entitled to nominate a tenant for the remaining part.
predicates.authorities_skipped_nomination_opportuni: The authorities allotted the vacant premises without first giving the landlord an opportunity to nominate a tenant.

issues.definition: If a rent-control vacancy allotment concerns premises for which the landlord is entitled to nominate a tenant, an allotment made without giving that opportunity is invalid.
